Question three. What is a race condition? It's when the result depends on the timing of operations on shared state. The classic case is a counter that two threads each add one to. Adding one isn't one step. It's three: read the value, add one, write it back. The counter is at five. Both threads read five, both add one, both write six. Two increments, and one is lost. Count every order those six steps can run in, and there are twenty. Only two of them give seven. The other eighteen lose an update. The fix is a lock around the three steps, so they run as one critical section. Then two orders are left, one thread first or the other, and both give seven. And since the bad orders depend on where a thread happens to pause, the same test can pass today and fail tomorrow, with no change to the code.

Question four. What is the gill, and why does it exist? In CPython, the standard Python interpreter, the global interpreter lock, or gill, is a single lock that lets only one thread run Python bytecode at a time. It exists to keep memory management thread-safe. Every object counts its references, and one lock around the interpreter protects all those counts without a lock on every object. The consequence: threads give no speedup to CPU-bound Python. They just take turns. They still help IO-bound work, because a thread releases the gill while it waits on the network or the disk. And it doesn't make the counter safe. The gill runs one bytecode instruction at a time, and that one line of Python compiles to four: load the counter, load the one, add, store. Nothing promises the four run together, so the lock is still needed. For CPU-bound work, use processes instead. Each has its own interpreter and its own gill, so they really do run in parallel.
